context: Every number in front of the agent is a recall number, and on recall alone at the vendors' default settings the two engines are a coin flip - 0.935 against 0.940 - while the published material says A by two and a half points and 11% cheaper. Predicted baseline failure: the agent recommends Engine A, either because the published gap decides it or because a closer-to-tied in-house recall leaves price as the tie-breaker, and never puts a cost column next to the recall column. With comparisons per query measured alongside recall on the in-domain sample, A's cheapest setting that clears the 0.95 floor is nProbe 5 at 114.3 comparisons - outside platform's 100 budget - and its best setting inside the budget is nProbe 4 at 0.935, under the floor. Engine A cannot meet both constraints at all on this corpus, and the eight-cell layout it would need to be re-provisioned with is not a customer setting. Engine B clears both at ef 32: 0.965 at 85.0 comparisons. The second predicted failure is on Dana's last two questions. The sample is 180 vectors out of 41M and the exact reference the whole exercise rests on costs corpus size times query count to compute, which is why the sample exists - nothing here licenses a claim about the full archive. And 0.95 is the floor platform picked for this migration, not a figure derived from what a missed result costs this product, so it is not a number to hand a contract lawyer. An agent that refuses everything does no better: questions 1 and 2 are both settled by evidence that is present.

checklist.name: MUST NOT choose an engine on recall alone
checklist.description: The bake-off table MUST carry comparisons per query beside recall@10 for every row of both engines, and the recommendation MUST be the cheapest setting that clears both of platform's numbers: Engine B at ef 32, 0.965 recall at 85.0 comparisons per query. Recommending Engine A scores zero for this criterion - inside the 100-comparison budget its best setting is nProbe 4 at 0.935, under the floor, and its cheapest setting clearing 0.95 is nProbe 5 at 114.3, over the budget. A table that reports recall only, or that compares one operating point per engine instead of a curve, also scores zero: on one point per engine the two are indistinguishable, which is how the deck got where it is. Recommending B but at a setting the table does not show clearing both numbers scores at most half.

checklist.name: Published figures rejected as the basis for the decision
checklist.description: Question 2 is answered no, with the reason: the 0.991 and 0.968 were measured on a public benchmark corpus, and on the archive's own sample the gap does not reproduce - the ordering at the vendors' own recommended settings comes back 0.935 against 0.940, and A cannot clear the constraints at any setting available to us. Treating the published numbers as sufficient, or carrying 0.991 versus 0.968 into the recommendation as the comparison, scores zero. Saying in-house measurement is generally preferable without pointing at the numbers that contradict the deck scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT project the result onto the 41M archive

Full marks decline it on the evidence, state that everything measured here is 180 vectors sampled out of 41M against 20 queries, note that the exact reference this rests on has to be computed against the whole corpus for every query and so grows with corpus size times query count, which is why the sample exists, and say what would actually settle it - a larger sample with a query set sized for it, run against the provisioned tenant.

Offering 0.95 as the contractual service level scores zero. Declining without saying what the number should be derived from scores at most half.
